UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, Plaintiff, v. KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6, Defendants. ____________________________________/ | Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S ADMINISTRATIVE MOTION FOR EXPEDITED BRIEFING, PRIORITY DETERMINATION, AND A DEFINED DECISION SCHEDULE FOR THE TWO RULE 26(d)(1) APPLICATIONS

I.	THE PRESENT CONSEQUENCE OF LEAVING TIMING UNRESOLVED

The Court has denied Plaintiff’s earlier requests for preconference discovery and has declined to direct ordinary scheduling and discovery planning while the dismissal motions remain pending. ECF No. 84 at 1–2; ECF No. 108 at 2. Plaintiff now presents two applications for present authorization of three defined interrogatory answers: Plaintiff’s Motion Under Rule 26(d)(1) for Present Authorization to Serve One Interrogatory on NCMEC Concerning Plaintiff’s Full Legal Name (ECF No. [___]) (the “NCMEC Application”) and Plaintiff’s Motion Under Rule 26(d)(1) for Present Authorization to Serve Two Interrogatories on Meta Concerning Plaintiff’s Full Legal Name and Facebook Account (ECF No. [___]) (the “Meta Application”). Those applications are supported by a declaration describing current effects on seeking counsel, participating professionally, conducting daily work, and attending to family responsibilities. Administrative Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine (“Admin. Decl.”) ¶¶ 5–12.

The administrative question is when those applications will be decided. A direction that motions will be determined on the papers identifies the mode of decision, not its timing. Docket Entry of Nov. 5, 2026 (“Per RDA’s chambers, motions set for 12/16/2026 will be decided on the papers; no oral argument will be heard.”). That entry addressed the motions then set for December 16 and supplied no decision date for these applications. Plaintiff requests seven-day opposition periods and three-day reply periods implemented through fixed calendar dates, submission without a hearing, and determination within seven days after each application becomes submitted.

Continued deferral leaves the challenged association public and the specified reporting questions unanswered while the consequences described in the declaration continue. Admin. Decl. ¶¶ 7, 9–12. Plaintiff requests a timetable directed to those consequences, not another prerequisite to consideration of the applications.

II.	THE APPLICATIONS SEEK DEFINED EXCEPTIONS, NOT GENERAL DISCOVERY

The NCMEC Application presents one question to Defendant National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (“NCMEC”):

Does NCMEC hold any CyberTipline report received from any reporting party between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, inclusive, that, as originally received by NCMEC, contained or otherwise identified the full legal name “Marvelle J. Ballentine”?

The Meta Application presents two independent questions to Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. (“Meta”):

Did Meta submit to NCMEC, between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, inclusive, any CyberTipline report that, as submitted by Meta, contained or otherwise identified the full legal name “Marvelle J. Ballentine”?

Did Meta submit to NCMEC, between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, inclusive, any CyberTipline report in connection with the Facebook account associated with Plaintiff and enforced against on or about July 4, 2022?

NCMEC’s question reaches reports from any reporting party. It is not confined to the two reports its April 22, 2026 letters mention. Meta’s first question is not confined to the specified account. Meta’s second question carries no full-name condition. The original-name restriction applies to the two name questions; later associations cannot supply original-report content. Meta answers its account question from its own submission records. Each question permits “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry,” a concise qualification necessary for accuracy, and specific objections under Rule 33(b)(4). None seeks report production, a narrative, a report number, a report date, or a submitter’s identity. NCMEC is the sole respondent to its interrogatory. Meta is the sole respondent to its two interrogatories. Defendant Katie Hall may oppose or join an opposition to the NCMEC Application; no interrogatory is directed to Hall.

Deciding whether to authorize those questions is one act. Conducting the searches, answering, and determining the later use of any answer are different acts, and each remains for the Applications and for later procedure. The requested schedule concerns only the first. A short permitted answer does not make the search costless; each Application addresses burden on its own record.

The operative pleading is the First Amended Complaint. ECF No. 5. It supplies the claims the Applications rest on. The pleading at ECF No. 114-2 is a proposed pleading accompanying a pending amendment motion and supplies no operative claim. ECF No. 116 is a separate request for an agency determination and alternative Rule 56(g) findings. Neither is a prerequisite to deciding whether to authorize three interrogatory answers.

The memoranda supporting the Applications (the “NCMEC Memorandum” and the “Meta Memorandum”) develop the Rule 26(d)(1) showings: the modified preliminary-injunction framework, NCMEC Mem. Part VII.B; Meta Mem. Part VII.B, and an independent good-cause ground, NCMEC Mem. Part VII.G; Meta Mem. Part VII.G. This memorandum identifies that function and leaves the discovery standards there. Neither Application requests shortened briefing through its own prayer for relief; this Administrative Motion requests that change on notice to all appearing parties, and the existing briefing periods govern unless the Court orders otherwise.

III.	THE COURT HAS AUTHORITY TO ESTABLISH THE REQUESTED SCHEDULE

Local Civil Rule 7(F)(1) supplies the ordinary periods: 14 calendar days after service for an opposition and six calendar days after service of the opposition for a reply, unless the Court directs otherwise. Its sentence excluding additional time for the method of service identifies those two periods. The fixed dates requested here are a different direction of the Court, and calendar dates raise no question of service-method additions.

Rule 78(b) provides that the Court may, by rule or order, provide for submitting and determining motions on briefs, without oral hearings. Local Civil Rule 7(J) supplies the local mechanism for waiver of oral argument. Plaintiff has waived oral argument on this Administrative Motion, and each Application carries its own waiver.

The Court’s authority to manage its docket supplies the rest. Dietz v. Bouldin, 579 U.S. 40, 45–47 (2016), recognizes a district court’s inherent power to manage its own affairs toward the orderly and expeditious disposition of cases, subject to two limits: the exercise must be a reasonable response to the problem before the court, and it cannot contradict an express rule or statute. District courts have “the inherent authority to manage their dockets and courtrooms with a view toward the efficient and expedient resolution of cases.” Id. at 47. The problem the schedule responds to is stated in Parts I and IV. No rule or statute forbids a shortened briefing period, a defined submission event, or a date certain for decision. Dietz supports the authority to set the schedule. It does not create an entitlement to a ruling within seven days, and Plaintiff does not cite it for one.

For the alternative routing, 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A) permits a district judge to designate a magistrate judge to hear and determine a pretrial matter pending before the court, subject to the exceptions stated there. Local Civil Rule 72 provides that duties may be referred to a magistrate judge by an order entered in the action or on the instructions of a district judge. An express referral of the two Applications, with authority to decide the requested exception, is within those provisions.

The Administrative Declaration is evidence on this Administrative Motion under Rule 43(c), which permits the Court to hear a motion on affidavits, and 28 U.S.C. § 1746, which permits an unsworn declaration under penalty of perjury in place of an affidavit. The declaration supports the timing request.

Rule 6 distinguishes a period computed from an event, which Rule 6(a) governs, from a fixed date set by the Court. The proposed orders use fixed dates. Rule 6(a) applies when the Court selects those dates, including its treatment of weekends and legal holidays. Plaintiff does not rely on Rule 6(b), which addresses extensions. Plaintiff does not invoke Rule 65, and this Administrative Motion need not satisfy the Applications’ modified preliminary-injunction framework; that showing belongs to the Applications.

IV.	PRESENT CONSEQUENCES JUSTIFY EXPEDITED ADJUDICATION

Four propositions connect the declaration to the requested timetable.

First, the declaration describes current effects, not litigation inconvenience. Plaintiff intends to retain counsel for his pending litigation and is reluctant to expose himself to another refusal while the association between his full legal name and CyberTipline reports remains unresolved. Admin. Decl. ¶¶ 6–7. The unresolved association affects his willingness to participate openly in professional networking, business development, incubators, accelerators, and founder fellowships, activities that involve his identity and professional credibility. Id. ¶¶ 8–10. The continuing uncertainty causes stress affecting his daily work, his family responsibilities, and his intended transition from handling the litigation himself to Docket Entry and his family. Id. ¶ 11. Those effects exist now.

Second, the historical refusal is context, not cause. About two years before November 7, 2026, Plaintiff was refused legal services. Admin. Decl. ¶ 5. He understood the refusal to be attributable, at least in part, to the child-sexual-exploitation designation associated with his Meta account. Id. That refusal occurred before NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters. Id. The letters did not cause that earlier refusal. The earlier experience explains why the present uncertainty bears on the present decision.

Third, the answers have a defined connection to the claims and a defined practical use. The NCMEC question tests the original-name component of the challenged association and NCMEC’s truth position concerning Counts I, II, and VI. Meta’s questions test the full-name and account-reporting relationships pleaded in Counts IV and V. NCMEC Mem. Parts VII.D.3, VII.F, VII.G; Meta Mem. Parts VII.D.3, VII.F, VII.G. The declaration explains why timely clarification matters to Plaintiff’s current decisions. Sworn organizational positions, given after reasonable inquiry, would inform his decisions about seeking counsel and participating openly in professional activities and would let him state what each organization has said from its own records. Admin. Decl. ¶ 12. Plaintiff promises no particular answer and does not contend that an answer will remove any public filing, procure counsel, or secure professional acceptance. The answers serve the existing claims and Plaintiff’s present decisions, and both uses depend on when the authorization requests are decided.

Fourth, timing matters independently of ultimate entitlement. A fully briefed authorization motion supplies no answer until it is decided and, if granted, implemented. The Applications’ own service and response terms run only after authorization. Accelerating briefing therefore addresses only part of the identified delay; a submission event and a decision date address the rest. Meta has proposed that Plaintiff seek discovery after his claims survive dismissal, and ECF No. 108 describes the deferral of ordinary discovery until the dismissal motions are resolved. ECF No. 73 at 4; ECF No. 108 at 2. On that sequence, ordinary discovery may end before an answer arrives. The requested timetable asks the Court to decide the exception requests while the consequences continue, whatever the decision is.

V.	THE PROPOSED SCHEDULE PRESERVES A MEANINGFUL RESPONSE OPPORTUNITY

Seven days is requested because the Applications concern reporting questions already litigated in this action. Defendants briefed the earlier interrogatory requests, ECF Nos. 15 and 54, which ECF No. 84 treated as requests for expedited discovery. ECF No. 84 at 1. The pending dismissal motions, ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45, are directed to the First Amended Complaint, which pleads the April 22, 2026 letters. ECF No. 89 ¶ 4. The legal-name subject appeared in the earlier requests.

The Applications nevertheless require a current response. Their scope has changed: one any-party, original-name question to NCMEC; two independent questions to Meta, one on original full-name content and one on the specified account. Their present-harm showing is new. Plaintiff does not describe the Applications as identical to the denied requests and does not argue that Defendants need no opportunity to address them. Seven days supplies that opportunity for a response directed to three defined questions and the accompanying sworn factual showing.

Two burdens must be kept apart. The seven-day opposition period concerns preparation of a response to the authorization request. It is not an order to complete the underlying reporting inquiry within that briefing period. Search capability, search steps, and response time are addressed in the Applications and, if authorization is granted, in the service and response terms the Court fixes. Nothing in this schedule shortens them, and nothing here assumes that either respondent has completed any search. The courtesy-copy request serves the schedule: a three-day reply operates only if Plaintiff, who is not a registered CM/ECF filer, receives each opposition when it is filed, and a contemporaneous electronic copy supplies that access without changing the method of service or supplying consent to electronic service.

[Complete from the November 9 conferral. If counsel for NCMEC and Hall or counsel for Meta proposed a different briefing period, state the period proposed and the reason given, separately for each: “Counsel for ___ proposed ___ days for opposition, stating ___.” If counsel stated no objection to the schedule, say so. If counsel took no position, say so. Do not invent a position.]

VI.	AN IDENTIFIED DECISION-MAKER AND A DEFINED ENDPOINT ARE NECESSARY

ECF No. 108 attributes the present deferral to the District Judge: “the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. Plaintiff describes the attribution as the order states it. His request to clarify or correct that passage, ECF Nos. 122–123, remains pending, and Plaintiff does not contend here that the source of the attributed instruction has been established. The attribution supplies the routing question. An application for a limited exception to a deferral attributed to the District Judge is one the District Judge can decide. A magistrate judge acting within a general pretrial referral may regard the exception as reserved. Either reading leaves the Applications in the same place unless the order says who decides them.

The requested order should answer that question. Primary relief: Judge Alston retains and determines both Applications. Alternative relief: an express referral under § 636(b)(1)(A) and Local Civil Rule 72 that authorizes the assigned Magistrate Judge to determine whether the deferral described in ECF No. 108 should permit the specific discovery requested, including service and response terms. Referral should allocate decision-making, not restart briefing or leave unresolved whether the referred judicial officer may decide the exception being requested. If the Magistrate Judge regards the exception as reserved, the order should direct the Magistrate Judge to state that understanding and present the request to the District Judge on the existing submissions. Local Civil Rule 72 also recognizes referral on the instructions of a district judge; the written routing provision requested here is case-management relief, not a claim that an entered order is the only form of referral or a claim to select a judicial officer. Plaintiff requests an order identifying the judicial officer authorized to determine the exception. Any reserved question should be presented to the District Judge on the existing submissions. Neither route requires decision of the historical referral questions in ECF Nos. 93 and 97–99 first, and Plaintiff does not ask for that.

The endpoint is the second half of the problem. Plaintiff requests determination of each Application within seven calendar days after that Application becomes submitted, or another date certain expressly fixed by the Court in the scheduling order. If the Court does not adopt the seven-day period, Plaintiff requests that the order state the substituted date and the reason for the departure. An undefined postponement would leave the timing question this Administrative Motion presents where it is now. The seven-day period is requested case-management relief, not a statutory deadline, and no grant, sanction, or finding follows from its passage. If shortened briefing can no longer operate prospectively when the Court acts, Plaintiff requests an order fixing submission, routing, and a determination date on the briefing as it then stands, without a further motion. Completed briefing remains complete.

VII.	COORDINATION WITHOUT SURRENDER OR DELAY

This request is consistent with the pending proceedings and displaces none of them. ECF No. 109 ¶ 11 asked the Court to preserve immediate determination of independent or threshold issues and independently warranted relief while the sequence requested there proceeds. The two Applications are independent of that sequence, and this Administrative Motion does not alter the order of consideration requested there. Plaintiff maintains ECF Nos. 89–90, 93, 97–99, 112–113, and 118–123 on their own grounds and reargues none of them here. The proposed pleading at ECF No. 114-2, the separate agency and Rule 56(g) request at ECF No. 116, and the settlement-referral proceedings at ECF Nos. 133–135 are not prerequisites to consideration of the Applications, and this Administrative Motion asks for no stay of anything. To the extent an adverse disposition would depend on the specific reporting fact addressed by an application’s Exhibit A, Plaintiff requests that the Court resolve that authorization request before or expressly within that disposition.

VIII.	CONCLUSION

Plaintiff requests entry of Proposed Order 4A: fixed opposition and reply dates for each Application, a defined submission event, determination within seven days after submission or on a date certain stated with its reason, determination retained by the District Judge, the narrow reporting-fact sequencing provision, prospective safeguards, and preservation of every other pending matter. In the alternative, Plaintiff requests Proposed Order 4B, which refers both Applications to the assigned Magistrate Judge with authority to decide the requested exception and with the same schedule. Only if the Court requires administrative submissions before ruling, Plaintiff requests Proposed Interim Order 4C. Plaintiff requests an order establishing when briefing will close, which judicial officer will determine each application, and when that determination will occur.
